newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapatistas defiant on anniversary of Mexico uprising.
newsitem.headline: Zapatistas defiant on anniversary of Mexico uprising.

text.p: On the third anniversary of their uprising, Mexico's Zapatista rebels on Wednesday issued a defiant statement that showed little hope of putting stalled peace talks back on track.

The Zapatistas walked out of negotiations four months ago, charging that the government was inflexible and racist. Aside from a one-day meeting in November the two sides have not held face-to-face talks since.

"If this fourth year is one of war or peace depends on whether the supreme power (President Ernesto Zedillo) accepts history and recognises the difference between his words and his actions," the statement said.
"This fourth year will be like all the years past and all the years to come: Live for the homeland or die for freedom," the statement said.
The rebel command remained holded up in the jungle of Mexico's southeastern Chiapas state, surrounded by the Mexican army as a ceasefire holds.
The Zapatista National Liberation Army stormed Chiapas three years ago on Wednesday, rattling the Mexican political system and capturing attention along the way.

In anticipation of the rebels' annual New Year's Day statement, the government's special peace commission, which began talks with the rebels 20 months ago, was hoping for some sign that peace talks could restart.

The peace commission was expecting a "message of encouragement for the nation" and hoped to "reach a mutual agreement on pacification in Mexico," Cesar Chavez, a government negotiator and congressman, told the newspaper Reforma.

In a separate statement from the New Year's message, the Zapatistas agreed to meet with government negotiators on Jan. 11-12, but only to review a previous accord on Indian rights and not to address an impasse over Mexican political reforms.

In Mexico City, supporters of the rebels held a music-filled festival marking the anniversary at a popular tourist plaza in the historic Coyoacan district. Rebel backers sold pro-Zapatista pamphlets and T-shirts, vying for space with the usual vendors of flowers and trinkets.

The Zapatistas, predominantly Maya Indians who had been training in the Chiapas jungle for years, introduced themselves to the world on Jan. 1, 1994, by seizing several of the major cities of Chiapas.

After 11 days of combat between guerrillas and government troops that killed an estimated 145 people, the government declared a unilateral ceasefire. Government and rebel delegations finally sat down together in April 1995 to start peace negotiations.
In the past three years, the Zapatistas have become the focus of sympathisers who supported the idea of an Indian-based guerrilla movement in the post-Cold War era.
Their central figure is the charismatic Subcommander Marcos, always seen wearing a ski mask and smoking a pipe.
In 1996, Marcos received such high-profile guests as film director Oliver Stone and Danielle Mitterrand, widow of the former French President Francois Mitterrand.

But critics say the Zapatistas' warm and fuzzy image is a facade, that the non-Inidan guerrilla leadership has always been a group of hard-core Marxists from the cities who played up the Maya cause only after their socialist rhetoric fell on deaf ears.
